comments.raw_comment:
What I Notice
The cost to make U.S. coins has increased a lot since 2001. In 2024, it costs 3.7 cents to make a penny, 13.8 cents to make a nickel, 5.8 cents to make a dime, and 14.7 cents to make a quarter. That means pennies and nickels actually cost more to make than they’re worth. The rise is especially sharp for nickels and quarters.
What I Wonder
I wonder why the cost to produce coins has gone up so much—especially for nickels. Is it because of rising metal prices, inflation, or changes in manufacturing? I also wonder if the government might stop producing pennies or change the materials to save money.
How This Relates to Me and My Community
Coins are still used in daily life, like vending machines or parking meters. If it costs more to make them than they’re worth, the government could raise taxes or cut costs elsewhere. Also, if pennies or nickels disappear, it could affect how stores price items or give change in my community.
Catchy Headline
“It Costs More to Make Money: Pennies and Nickels Lose Their Value in Production”

In this graph, I notice four different charts showing the mint cost for all coins. The penny and Nickel charts are shown in red, indicating that their production costs exceed their face values. The dime and quarter charts are shown in grey, with their production costs lower than their values. The cost of minting all coins has risen sharply since 2001. Does the value of the penny become nothing after production ceases, or it its value rise dramatically? This issue connects to my community because coins are still used in everyday places like vending machines, laundromats, and parking meters. If certain coins were eliminated, it could affect local businesses and daily transactions.

They are represented by a red line once it passes the dotted line indicating the coin's value. I also observe that manufacturing costs have increased moderately, with a significant rise across the board around 2009/10, before decreasing and then starting to rise again. I wonder why these costs fluctuate so often. I also question whether the discrepancy between the cost and value of pennies and nickels means production of nickels might stop soon, since they plan to stop making pennies. Will they change materials instead? This impacts me and my community because it directly reflects the nation's economic state. What do you notice?
I noticed how coins that hold less value, such as the pennie and nickel, production prices have inflated much more that the dime or quarter in relation to their original value. The starting values of the coins production is also much lower in the dime and quarter than it is for the pennie and nickel, meaning that since those coins hold less value, it is more difficult to produce them to prices that match or are below their value. I also noticed that all of the lines of each coins price to produce mirror each other and spike and decline at similar rates. 
What do you wonder?
What has caused these massive spikes in the coins' production, doubling the cost of making pennies and nickels, and significantly raising the price of making quarters and dimes? I also wonder what economic situations have occurred that have led to these major spikes or declines in the price of production. If this affects the value of my coin, and if it costs 5 cents to make, why is it worth 1 cent?
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community because coins are still a prominent currency today, and if they cost more to produce than their value, then how does this affect the worth of my penny? It also may affect the proceeds of distribution and production of coins, which may affect how coins are used today, thus affecting my community and me.

comments.raw_comment: In this graph I notice four different graphs showing how much it costs to create each coin. The penny and the nickels graph is red, while the dime and quarters line is grey. This is because in the graph there is a grey dotted line representing the worth of each coin. If the statistic line is over the dotted line then it is red, displaying that the government is losing money by creating these coins. For instance a nickel is worth 5  cents but to produce one nickel it costs 13.8 cents in production. The graph is also showcasing how the price of manufacturing has changed from 2001 to 2024. I wonder why each coin has become more expensive to produce? Is it because the materials are more expensive or because inflation is causing the price of money to go down? I also wonder if the government will get rid of pennies and nickels because they are causing the government to lose money, I know that this has been talked about before. This relates to my community because it is causing the government to lose lots of money on things that are not that important, such as a penny. This affects the economy which ultimately affects all the citizens, such as me and my family. All in all a catchy headline for this graph could be, “Do We Really Need Pennies?”

1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?
I noticed that the amount it costs to manufacture each coin spiked around 2010, went back down, but is now on the rise again. I also noticed that it costs the government more than the coins are worth for pennies and nickels, the coins with the least amount of value. 

2. What do you wonder?
 I wonder if it is were it for the government to still manufacture these coins that have such little value when it costs more to make than what the coins are actually worth.

3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
The impact this has on me and my community is the way we use physical money. I think Americans find themselves using change less and less, so if the government stopped making some of it altogether, there wouldn't be that great of an impact on people's lives, but we would see the impact in the economy. If the government stopped making one-cent and five-cent coins, I think that there would be a significant amount of inflation, and since the dime would become the new lowest value coin, it would become the new lowest value.

comments.raw_comment:
Looking at this graph, as lines go up, up, up, I notice the label of coins. Connecting this with the ever increasing line that is given, I can see that the price it takes to make these value coins are skyrocketing. Looking at the cost of this production increase makes me wonder why we keep using coins and why we can’t fix this problem. I think I understand that the price goes up as the source for materials we need decreases due to supply and demand. This relates to me and my community because this causes inflation in the economy. This affects all prices of products that me and my community use and buy. It also affects people when we simply go out to eat with each other and see menu prices increase. Going on a date or hanging out with friends to get a drink, where we see drinks increased from $5 to $7. Especially for teenagers like myself, it’s hard with inflation like these, we don’t have as much of an income or we don’t have an income at all to be able to hang out with our friends. This can also tie into small businesses having a hard time surviving with little workers. As it is equally as hard to be able to fund labor and pay workers, teenagers can struggle with getting jobs as it’s hard to provide pay.

A Nguyen, FVHS

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that the cost to produce U.S. coins had increased over the past two decades, especially for pennies and nickels. By 2024, it costs 3.7 cents to make a penny and 13.8 cents to make a nickel, meaning these coins cost a lot more to produce than they are worth. Dimes and quarters have also become more expensive to mint, but they still cost less than their face value.

What do you wonder?
I wonder why the government continues to produce coins that cost more than their own value, especially pennies and nickels. I also wonder how much taxpayers, can actually  pay for this and whether inflation and rising metal prices are the main causes. Will the U.S. eventually stop producing pennies, or switch to different materials to reduce cost?

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that the coins with lower values like the penny and the nickel have become not cost-effective to make, since the cost to produce them is greater than their value, whereas higher-valued coins like dimes and quarters are worth about twice as much as it costs to make them. It’s also interesting that nickels cost almost 15¢ to make (almost as much as the quarter) while being worth only 5¢. There is also a noticeable drop in the cost to produce coins around 2020 when the pandemic was happening. Based on the political and economic state of the world right now, it seems that the trend of increasing cost will only go up as we accrue more debt and inflation rises, but I wonder whether this will actually happen or if we’ll turn the economy around. I also wonder what will happen to prices as we phase out coins like the penny (and presumably the nickel later), since prices will be rounded up to the nearest 0.10¢ since pennies and nickels will no longer be in circulation. Alternatively, people will most likely start paying with card rather than cash in order to make sure that they only have to pay as much as they need. Since we’ll only have coins that pay themselves off, the government will save a lot of money and can use it for other things.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that the penny and the nickel are quickly becoming more costly to produce than they are worth, with the nickel especially being far more expensive (almost matching the quarter). There also seems to be a dip around 2020 among all the coins, where they actually became cheaper instead of continuing the trend of increasing cost.

I wonder what the full graph for a longer time period would look like, and also whether the trend of phasing out coins (like the penny) will continue until we only use dollar bills.

This could cause prices to rise slightly for every product over time, as it would be illogical for prices to end in .99 if pennies are no longer in circulation, or for prices to end in .05, if nickels do not exist (and it is very unlikely that corporations—or anyone for that matter—would opt to round down their prices, rather than round up). Although the numbers are very small, they do add up over time given the amount of products the average consumer purchases. The middle-class and people with stable incomes likely won’t be as affected, since these people also generally pay with card rather than cash, but those less fortunate may have to create an even stricter budget to afford the most basic products. Another factor would also be the effect it has on taxpayer money, as phasing out coins that do not pay themselves off would save lots of money that could be redirected for more useful expenditures.

Will the Nickel follow the Penny?

comments.raw_comment: Something that I noticed about the graph is the cost of what it takes to make a nickel and how it breaks the general trend of the relationship between coin value and cost to make. Despite the nickel being one of the least used coins, its cost to create brings up the essential question of whether or not we should continue the minting of nickels and whether or not to abolish it as a whole. Furthermore, as the use of app payment or cards increase in communities such my very own, the thought of using physical currency such as coins becomes an afterthought or even a nuisance in daily life as many people would rather give away or toss their change aside. Tying back to the question asked earlier, the fact that a nickel costs more to produce than a quarter and that coins are becoming increasingly less used in our daily lives, the idea of halting the production of nickel becomes less of a radical idea. Lastly, a head line that I’d give for this graph is, “Are Nickels Worth More Than a Quarter?”
